title: What is the purpose of using Views in SQL (simplify queries, reusability, security, abstraction, logical independence, readability, reporting)?
shortTitle: Purpose of Using Views in SQL

s1_definition.profdef: A view is a named, stored `SELECT` query that behaves like a virtual table: it holds no data of its own but presents the result of its underlying query whenever it is referenced. Its purposes are to simplify complex queries, enable reuse, enforce security by exposing only selected columns and rows, provide abstraction and logical independence from the base tables, improve readability, and support consistent reporting.
s1_definition.analogy: A view is like a pre-approved National Bank of India report template. Instead of every clerk re-deriving "active accounts with balance over ten thousand" from raw tables each time, the bank defines that report once, names it, and everyone just runs the named report. Tellers only ever see the columns the template exposes — not the sensitive raw columns behind it — so it also acts as a controlled window.
s1_definition.oneliner: A view is a stored query acting as a virtual table — it simplifies, reuses, secures, and abstracts access to the underlying data without duplicating it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A view is a named, stored `SELECT` query that behaves like a virtual table: it holds no data of its own but presents the result of its underlying query whenever it is referenced. Its purposes are to simplify complex queries, enable reuse, enforce security by exposing only selected columns and rows, provide abstraction and logical independence from the base tables, improve readability, and support consistent reporting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A view is like a pre-approved National Bank of India report template. Instead of every clerk re-deriving "active accounts with balance over ten thousand" from raw tables each time, the bank defines that report once, names it, and everyone just runs the named report. Tellers only ever see the columns the template exposes — not the sensitive raw columns behind it — so it also acts as a controlled window.

**One line to remember:** A view is a stored query acting as a virtual table — it simplifies, reuses, secures, and abstracts access to the underlying data without duplicating it.

sections.s2_technical:
A view is defined with `CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...`. It stores only the query definition, not rows, so every time you query the view the database runs the underlying `SELECT` (optionally merging it into your outer query for optimization). This gives several concrete benefits. First, simplification: a gnarly multi-join, multi-filter query can be wrapped once in a view so callers write `SELECT * FROM active_premium_accounts` instead of repeating the joins. Second, reusability: the same logic is defined once and used by many reports, services, and users, so a change to the business rule is made in one place.

Third, security: a view can expose only certain columns (hiding sensitive ones like full account numbers or salaries) and only certain rows (via a `WHERE`), and you can grant users access to the view while denying access to the base tables — a classic way to implement column- and row-level security. Fourth, abstraction and logical independence: callers depend on the view's shape, not the physical table layout, so you can refactor or split base tables and simply update the view definition to keep the interface stable. Fifth, readability and consistency: named views make queries self-documenting and ensure everyone computes a metric the same way, which is vital for reporting where different ad-hoc queries could otherwise produce different numbers.

Important nuances to mention as a senior: a plain view is computed on every access, so it is always fresh but carries the cost of its query each time; for heavy aggregations you may use a materialized view that stores the result. Views can be updatable if simple enough (single table, no aggregation), but complex views are read-only unless you add `INSTEAD OF` triggers. In some engines `WITH CHECK OPTION` prevents inserts or updates through the view that would fall outside its `WHERE`. Views do not inherently improve performance (the underlying query still runs), so they are primarily about structure, safety, and clarity rather than speed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India has a wide `accounts` table containing sensitive columns (full account number, customer PAN) alongside ordinary ones. Reporting staff need to see only active accounts with a masked account number and the balance, and they must never touch the raw table. Separately, multiple dashboards kept re-deriving "active premium accounts" with slightly different filters, producing inconsistent numbers.

Our mini-project models a base table and a `View` abstraction that stores a query definition (projection + filter), proving that querying the view runs the stored logic live, exposes only safe columns, and gives every caller identical, consistent results — demonstrating simplification, security, reuse, and abstraction.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four accounts with a mix of statuses and tiers, each carrying sensitive columns (full account number and PAN) plus ordinary ones.

Step 1 — A view named `active_premium_accounts` is defined once, storing a `WHERE` (status is ACTIVE and tier is PREMIUM) and a projection that masks the account number and exposes only tier and balance. It stores no data, just this definition.

Step 2 — A caller runs `SELECT * FROM active_premium_accounts`. The view executes its stored query live against the base table rather than returning any cached rows.

Step 3 — The filter keeps only active premium accounts, dropping the closed premium account and the standard account, demonstrating row-level security and consistent business logic.

Step 4 — The projection exposes a masked account number, tier, and balance, and deliberately omits the full account number and PAN, demonstrating column-level security and abstraction — the caller never sees or depends on the sensitive raw columns.

Step 5 — Every caller that uses this view gets identical rows computed the same way, giving reuse and consistent reporting; a change to the rule would be made once in the view.

Final output:

```text
SELECT * FROM active_premium_accounts;
  {account_masked=XXXXXX7890, tier=PREMIUM, balance=85000.0}
  {account_masked=XXXXXX2211, tier=PREMIUM, balance=150000.0}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  base table: accounts (accountNo, pan, status, tier, balance)  [sensitive+ordinary]
        │
        │  CREATE VIEW active_premium_accounts (stored query, no data)
        ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WHERE status=ACTIVE AND tier=PREMIUM (filter) │  ← row security + consistent rule
  │ SELECT mask(accountNo), tier, balance (proj)  │  ← column security (pan hidden)
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │  caller: SELECT * FROM view  (runs live each time)
        ▼
  masked, filtered rows — identical for every caller (reuse, reporting)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — View Abstraction ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Decorator/Facade: view wraps base table with filter + projection  │
  │ Strategy: WHERE predicate and projection are pluggable            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: view only filters+projects; base table only stores            │
  │ O: new view = new predicate/projection, base untouched           │
  │ I: callers see only exposed columns                              │
  │ D: callers depend on view, not physical table layout             │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Plain vs materialized (preview) ──
  plain view       : computed every access, always fresh, no storage
  materialized view: stored snapshot, fast reads, can be stale

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │          SqlView             │ ─────▶ │  Account (base row)  │
  │ - where: Predicate           │  reads │ - accountNo/pan      │
  │ - projection: Function       │        │ - status/tier/balance│
  │ + query(base): List<Map>     │        └──────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  1. Demo.main()  [CREATE VIEW: predicate + safe projection]
  2.   → query(accounts)  [filter: ACTIVE & PREMIUM]
  3.       → projection    [mask accountNo, drop pan]
  4.   → return masked consistent rows
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A view is a named, stored `SELECT` query that behaves like a virtual table: it holds no rows of its own and instead runs its underlying query whenever it is referenced. Its purposes cover several distinct needs. It simplifies queries by wrapping a complex multi-join, multi-filter statement once so callers write a single clean `SELECT` against the view. It enables reuse because the logic is defined in one place and shared by many services and reports, so a rule change happens once. It enforces security by exposing only chosen columns and rows — you can hide sensitive columns like a full account number or PAN, restrict rows with a `WHERE`, and grant users access to the view while denying access to the base tables, giving column- and row-level security. It provides abstraction and logical independence because callers depend on the view's stable shape rather than the physical table layout, so you can refactor base tables and just update the view. And it improves readability and consistent reporting because a named view is self-documenting and guarantees everyone computes a metric the same way.

At the National Bank of India, our `accounts` table mixed sensitive columns with ordinary ones, and several dashboards kept re-deriving "active premium accounts" with slightly different filters, producing conflicting numbers. We defined one view, `active_premium_accounts`, that filtered to active premium rows and exposed only a masked account number, tier, and balance, then granted reporting staff access to the view alone. That single change simplified every report, guaranteed consistent figures, and ensured no report could reach the PAN or full account number. The senior nuances I always add are that a plain view is recomputed on each access so it is always fresh but not a performance shortcut, that simple single-table views can be updatable while complex ones need `INSTEAD OF` triggers, that `WITH CHECK OPTION` stops writes that would escape the view's filter, and that when an expensive aggregation must be fast you reach for a materialized view instead. The line I always state is that a view is a stored query acting as a virtual table that simplifies, reuses, secures, and abstracts access to data without duplicating it.

keyPoints: Stored procedure: precompiled SQL code on the DB server
Views: virtual table from a SELECT — simplify complex queries
Pros: performance, security. Cons: hard to version, test, debug
